To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) a new method was developed to extract structural features of DNA-drug complexes and (2) a statistical model was built to predict the interaction strength of small-molecule agents to DNA.
(1) a novel structural feature-based predictor for DNA–drug binding affinity was developed and (2) the binding behavior of small-molecule agents with their DNA targets was investigated.

(1) a novel structural feature extraction method is proposed and used to develop a DNA–drug affinity predictor, (2) the predictor is employed to examine the binding specificity and selectivity of a large pool of DNA–drug complexes and decoy systems, and (3) the results reveal the physicochemical origin and thermodynamic profile for sequence-specific interactions in the recognition of DNA by small-molecule ligand.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a new method of analyzing the structural features of a DNA–drug complex, a statistical model of predicting the affinity of DNA–drug binding, and the application of these tools in understanding the sequence-specific interaction between DNA and small-molecule drugs.
the molecular recognition mechanism of a series of drug compounds with their DNA receptors, which are important for understanding the biological activity of these compounds.
the structural and energetic insights into the DNA–drug recognition process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DNA–drug recognition is a rather weakly sequence-specific interaction, which may be a result of a relatively small number of DNA-binding drugs and a limited set of DNA sequences used in this study.
the binding affinity of DNA–drug complexes is determined by the structural features of the DNA receptor, and the selectivity of the drug ligand is determined by the sequence of the DNA receptor.

DNA–drug recognition is a relatively loose process in comparison with protein–DNA interaction and that the specificity of drug–DNA recognition is largely determined by the sequence of the DNA receptor rather than the chemical structure of the drug ligands.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DNA–drug recognition mechanism is more complicated than previously thought.
the DNA–drug recognition mechanism is different from that of protein–DNA interactions, and that the binding of a drug to DNA is a relatively nonselective and nonspecific process.

, in contrast with the highly specific protein–DNA interactions, DNA–drug interactions are relatively non-specific and the binding selectivity of a small-molecule agent for its cognate DNA receptor is determined primarily by the abundance of A and T nucleotides in the core DNA sequence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the specificity of small-molecule agents in selecting their cognates from the background of random decoys is not as strong as that of protein ligands.
the specificity of DNA–drug interactions may be less pronounced than that of protein–DNA interactions.
DNA–drug recognition is a less specific process than protein–DNA recognition in terms of sequence selectivity.
